warmup.q: The quote service answers within 300 ms. Northline takes 10 calls at a time and needs 50 ms per call. A burst of 500 requests arrives at once, and the service lets them all queue. About how many get a live Northline price?
options: All 500, each a little later than usual
About 50 to 60: ten at a time, and six rounds of 50 ms fit in 300 ms
None: the burst knocks Northline over
warmup.why: Little's law: 10 calls at once at 50 ms each is at most 200 calls a second, so 300 ms holds about 60. This lesson's demo got 50, because the sixth round ends exactly at the deadline. The other 450 wait for a permit until their deadline and then fail. Queueing them didn't get them a price; it made them slow failures. Section 4 turns them into fast ones.

opening:
Picture the post office on the last day before the holidays. The queue runs out of the door, and everyone wants a price at once. The three couriers behind the counter have limits of their own. Northline's contract allows ten questions at a time, and one of its answers in twenty is very slow. Eastgate sometimes says "try again later". And Fjord holds a seat on a van every time it's asked.

The easy trap is to let every customer in and hope. Each request then waits its full deadline for a courier that was never going to answer, and the service looks slow when the truth is that it's full.

Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline asked the three couriers at once, under one deadline. In this lesson, we'll give each courier its own limit, repeat only the questions that are safe to repeat, send a second question when one is slow, turn customers away at the door with a clear word, and close at night without losing a coroutine. Then we'll ask whether one virtual thread per customer would have been simpler. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started on the post office's busiest day. Now each courier gets its share of calls, only harmless questions are asked twice, a slow answer gets a second chance, and a customer we can't serve hears "busy" at once.

That's Part 2 in one program: the bakery's slip became auto-read, the cook texted the couriers under a kitchen timer, the shelf chose what to lose, and the clerk never picked up the phone.

Search your code for a retry around a call that books or charges something.

Next, we'll start Part 3 with Generics from zero, in a fruit shop's storeroom. Our service kept promises about time. Can a label on a box make the compiler keep promises about types?

sections.h: A bulkhead for each courier, sized by Little's law
sections.html:
Lesson 2's fan-out sends every request to every courier at once. With a thousand requests in flight, Northline sees a thousand calls at once, and its contract allows 10. Past that, it answers 429, the web's code for "too many requests", or it slows down for everyone.

The fix is a bulkhead, named after the walls inside a ship's hull that keep one flooded section from sinking the whole ship. Here, it's a limit on the calls in flight to one courier, so that one courier's limit can't become everybody's outage. Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores pictured it as twenty tokens by the grill: a pan goes on only with a token in hand, and a cook without one waits. A semaphore is that box of tokens, and each token is a permit.

In the lab, the guards for one courier live in GuardedProvider, a wrapper that applies them and then passes each call on to the real courier. Its bulkhead is a Semaphore from kotlinx.coroutines.sync:

Java
// Java equivalent on virtual threads: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, acquire before the try
private Quote once(String destination) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();                                             // blocks a cheap virtual thread
    try {
        return delegate.quote(destination);
    } finally {
        permits.release();
    }
}
Kotlin
class GuardedProvider(private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int /* ... */) : Provider {
    private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent)                 // kotlinx.coroutines.sync

    private suspend fun once(destination: String): Quote =
        permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(destination) }         // suspends while all permits are out
}

withPermit takes a permit, runs the call and gives the permit back, however the call ends. While no permit is free, it suspends. It holds no thread, and the wait is cancellable, so lesson 2's deadline still applies: a call that waits too long for a permit is cancelled with the rest and counts as no answer. The Java twin does the same with the JDK's Semaphore on a virtual thread, where waiting is cheap too.

How many permits? Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law gave the rule: the calls in flight equal the arrival rate times the time per call. If Northline allows 10 calls at once and answers in 50 ms, it serves at most 10 / 0.05 = 200 calls a second. More permits add no speed. They only move the queue to Northline's side, where you can't see it. So take the number from each courier's contract, and give each courier its own: Eastgate allows 40 and Fjord 5, as the figure shows.

This section's demo sends 40 requests at once to a courier that answers in 50 ms. With no limit, the courier sees all 40 at once, and every answer arrives after 50 ms. With a limit of 4, it never sees more than 4, and the 40 answers take 10 rounds of 50 ms, 500 ms in all. The limit didn't make anything faster. It made the courier's load a number we chose.

Two placement rules matter. The permit goes around each single call, not around a whole retry loop: a call that waits out its pause before a retry shouldn't hold a permit meanwhile, and a hedge, the second call of section 3, needs a permit of its own. And the bulkhead lives in the courier's wrapper, not around the fan-out. A limit on requests can't protect a courier, because each request makes three calls.

A courier's limit is a number in its contract. Write it into a semaphore, around every single call.

Now each courier sees no more than its share. Some of those calls still fail, and the question is whether to ask again.

try.title: Forty requests, one courier, two limits
steps: Open BulkheadDemo.kt (virtual time) or BulkheadDemoJava.java (virtual threads, real time). Forty requests call a courier that answers in 50 ms.
Predict the most calls in flight at once, and the time until all forty are answered, with no limit and with a limit of 4.
Run it. Then change the limit to 8 and predict again from Little's law.

code.title: BulkheadDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? */ fun main() = runTest { // virtual time, one thread: plain counters are safe here for (limit in listOf(null, 4)) { val permits = limit?.let { Semaphore(it) } var active = 0 var peak = 0 suspend fun call() { active++ peak = maxOf(peak, active) delay(50) // the provider thinks active-- } val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(40) { launch { if (permits == null) call() else permits.withPermit { call() } } } } println("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms".format( if (limit == null) "no limit" else "limit $limit", peak, currentTime - t0)) } }

alt.title: BulkheadDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent with virtual threads: one per request, and a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore as the bulkhead package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? Real time. */ public class BulkheadDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer limit : new Integer[] {null, 4}) { Semaphore permits = limit == null ? null : new Semaphore(limit); AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable call = () -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } active.decrementAndGet(); }; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (permits == null) { call.run(); return null; } permits.acquire(); // acquire before the try try { call.run(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all 40 System.out.printf("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms%n", limit == null ? "no limit" : "limit " + limit, peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } }

try.expect: No limit: 40 calls at once, all answered after 50 ms. Limit 4: 4 at once, and 40 / 4 = 10 rounds of 50 ms, 500 ms. With a limit of 8, it is 5 rounds, 250 ms. The Java twin prints the same peaks in real time, with a few extra milliseconds of scheduling (81 and 511 ms in one run on a busy machine). The limit didn't make anything faster; it made the courier's load a number you chose.

sections.h: Retry only what is safe to repeat, and spread the retries out
sections.html:
A transient failure, one that goes away by itself, often succeeds on a second try: a 503, the web's code for "busy, try again later", or a connection that broke halfway. But a retry, asking again after a failure, is a second request, and the courier can't tell it from a new one.

That matters more for some couriers than others. Northline and Eastgate only look up a price, so asking twice changes nothing. Fjord's price is a booking: each call holds a place on one of its vans for two minutes and counts against our daily allowance of calls. Ask Fjord twice, and it holds two places. A call is idempotent when repeating it does no harm, like reading a price. So the decision belongs to the courier, as Provider.idempotent, which is false unless the courier says otherwise:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: the same decision before any retry operator is added
Mono<Quote> quote(String destination) {
    Mono<Quote> once = Mono.defer(() -> delegate.quote(destination));
    if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once;                       // a booking: exactly one call
    return once.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.5)
            .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException));
}
Kotlin
override suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote {
    val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(destination) } }   // 1. a permit per call
    if (!delegate.idempotent) return once()                         // 2. a booking: exactly one call
    val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) })
    return retrying(backoff, random, attempt)                       // 3. the rest may be asked again
}

Let's read it in order. Every single call holds a permit (1). A courier that isn't idempotent gets exactly one call (2). The rest go through retrying, with a hedge around each attempt when one is set (3).

retrying is the retry loop with growing waits from Shared state and testing coroutines, a backoff, with one change: jitter. When Northline has a bad moment, every request in flight fails in the same millisecond. Without jitter, they all come back one backoff later, punctual to the millisecond, and hit a courier that is still getting back on its feet. Jitter multiplies each wait by a random factor, here between 0.5 and 1.5, which spreads the retries out. Reactor's Retry.backoff does the same by default, as Errors, retries and timeouts showed:

Java
// Java equivalent on a virtual thread: the same factor, and a sleep that an interrupt ends
double factor = 1 + jitter * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1);
Thread.sleep((long) (nominal(n).toMillis() * factor));
Kotlin
val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1)   // 0.5 .. 1.5 for jitter 0.5
delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor)                                  // cancellable: the deadline still rules

It's the broken oven from that lesson, with a crowd of packers. If every packer asks for the tray to be baked again at the same second, the oven that has just been repaired breaks again.

This section's demo has 1,000 customers that failed together and retry after a nominal 100 ms. Without jitter, all 1,000 retries land in one millisecond. With a jitter of 0.5, they spread over 50 to 150 ms, and no millisecond gets more than 18.

Three more rules keep retries honest. Retry only errors that a later attempt might fix: here an IOException, never an unknown destination. Keep every wait cancellable, so the deadline cuts off retries that can't finish in time; a retry after the deadline is work nobody will read. And count the calls. Two retries means up to three calls per request, and Little's law counts every one of them.

A retry is a second request. Send it only when repeating is harmless, and never all at the same moment.

Retries help when a call fails. Some calls don't fail at all. They're just slow.

try.title: A thousand retries in one millisecond
steps: Open RetryJitterDemo.kt (or the Java twin, which computes the same waits without sleeping). A thousand customers failed together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms.
Predict how the retries spread over 25 ms buckets with no jitter and with a jitter of 0.5, and the most retries in any single millisecond.
Run it. Then set the jitter to 0.1 and predict the busiest millisecond.

code.title: RetryJitterDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlin.random.Random import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ fun main() = runTest { for (jitter in listOf(0.0, 0.5)) { val random = Random(7) val retryAt = IntArray(1_000) val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(1_000) { client -> launch { val factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(100.milliseconds * factor) retryAt[client] = (currentTime - t0).toInt() } } } val buckets = retryAt.groupBy { it / 25 * 25 }.toSortedMap() println("jitter $jitter: " + buckets.entries.joinToString(" ") { (from, hits) -> "$from-${from + 24} ms: ${hits.size}" }) println(" most retries in one millisecond: ${retryAt.groupBy { it }.values.maxOf { it.size }}") } }

alt.title: RetryJitterDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent: the same jitter formula with java.util.Random; the waits are computed, not slept package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; import java.util.TreeMap; /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ public class RetryJitterDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { for (double jitter : new double[] {0.0, 0.5}) { Random random = new Random(7); Map<Integer, Integer> buckets = new TreeMap<>(); Map<Integer, Integer> perMs = new TreeMap<>(); for (int client = 0; client < 1_000; client++) { double factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1); // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter int at = (int) Math.ceil(100 * factor); // delay rounds up to whole ms buckets.merge(at / 25 * 25, 1, Integer::sum); perMs.merge(at, 1, Integer::sum); } StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder("jitter " + jitter + ":"); buckets.forEach((from, hits) -> line.append(String.format(" %d-%d ms: %d", from, from + 24, hits))); System.out.println(line); System.out.println(" most retries in one millisecond: " + perMs.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().orElse(0)); } } }

try.expect: No jitter: all 1,000 retries in the 100 to 124 ms bucket, and all of them in the same millisecond. Jitter 0.5: about 250 in each bucket from 50 to 149 ms (a few land at exactly 150 after rounding up), and the busiest millisecond has 18 (17 in the Java twin, whose random numbers differ). With 0.1, the retries squeeze into 90 to 110 ms, and the busiest millisecond gets about three times as many: less jitter, less spread.

sections.h: Hedge the slow tail of one courier
sections.html:
Northline answers in 40 ms most of the time, but one call in twenty takes 600 ms. Nothing failed, so a retry doesn't help. Northline is simply lost in thought now and then.

To talk about slow calls, we need one more word. A percentile says how slow the slow ones are: p50 is the time half the calls beat, and p99 is the time 99 calls in 100 beat. The slowest few calls are the tail, and tail latency is what the unluckiest customers see. Northline's p50 is 40 ms. Its p99 is 600 ms.

A hedge cuts the tail. If the first call hasn't answered by the time 95 calls in 100 would have (its p95), send one more identical call and take whichever answers first. It's the cook texting a second branch of the same shop when the first hasn't replied by the time shops usually do:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: the delayed hedge is cancelled before it starts if the first call wins
Mono<Quote> hedged(Duration after, Mono<Quote> call) {
    return Mono.firstWithValue(call, Mono.delay(after).then(call));
}
Kotlin
suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope {
    val first = async { call() }                               // 1. the first call
    val early = withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() }     // 2. stops the waiting, not the call
    if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early
    val second = async { call() }                              // 3. the hedge
    val winner = select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } }
    coroutineContext.cancelChildren()                          // 4. stop the loser
    winner
}

Let's read it in order. We start the first call (1). withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } stops waiting at the hedge time (2), and it doesn't cancel first, which is a child of the coroutineScope, not of the timeout. If nothing came back, we start the hedge (3). select takes whichever deferred completes first, the way Channels, select and pipelines took whichever answer came first. Then cancelChildren() stops the loser (4). Forget that line, and coroutineScope waits for the slow call anyway, which undoes the hedge.

This section's demo asks Northline for 200 prices, one after another, first without a hedge and then with a hedge after 80 ms. On virtual time it printed:

no hedge        p50  40 ms   p99 600 ms   max 600 ms   calls to Northline: 200
hedge at 80 ms  p50  40 ms   p99 120 ms   max 120 ms   calls to Northline: 210

The p99 fell from 600 ms to 120 ms: 80 ms of waiting, plus 40 ms for the hedge. It cost 10 extra calls, 5% more, because only the slow 5% got a hedge.

That cost decides where hedges go. Hedge only an idempotent courier, because a hedge is a duplicate request: a hedged Fjord would book two vans. Hedge only the courier whose tail hurts, here Northline, at a time taken from its measured latency. And make the hedge take its own permit from the bulkhead. When Northline is saturated, a hedge would only add to the queue that made it slow, so under full load the hedge waits for a permit, and the first call usually wins. The lab has a test for exactly that: with one permit, the hedge never runs alongside the first call.

A hedge is a duplicate request. Spend it on the slow tail, and only where a duplicate is harmless.

Bulkheads, retries and hedges look after the couriers and the customer's wait. Nothing yet protects the service itself from more customers than it can answer.

steps: Open HedgeDemo.kt. Northline answers in 40 ms, except every 20th call, which takes 600 ms. The demo asks for 200 prices without a hedge, then with a hedge after 80 ms.
Predict p50, p99, the slowest request and the number of calls for both runs.
Run it. Then set the hedge to 30 ms, below Northline's normal time, and predict the number of calls.

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.firstWithValue races the call against a hedge that starts after 80 ms package workbench.quotes.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 200 quotes from Northline, all at once, with and without a hedge after 80 ms. Real time. */ public class HedgeDemoJava { static final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); // Northline: 40 ms, except every 20th call, which takes 600 ms (its slow 5%) static Mono<String> northline() { return Mono.defer(() -> { int n = calls.incrementAndGet(); return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(n % 20 == 0 ? 600 : 40)).thenReturn("northline 12.45"); }); } static Mono<String> hedged(Duration after) { // the delayed hedge is cancelled before it starts if the first call answers in time return Mono.firstWithValue(northline(), Mono.delay(after).then(northline())); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Duration hedgeAfter : new Duration[] {null, Duration.ofMillis(80)}) { calls.set(0); List<Long> latencies = Flux.range(1, 200) .flatMap(i -> { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Mono<String> q = hedgeAfter == null ? northline() : hedged(hedgeAfter); return q.map(x -> (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); }, 200) .sort() .collectList().block(); System.out.printf("%-15s p50 %3d ms p99 %3d ms max %3d ms calls to Northline: %d%n", hedgeAfter == null ? "no hedge" : "hedge at 80 ms", latencies.get(99), latencies.get(197), latencies.get(199), calls.get()); } } }

try.expect: No hedge: p50 40 ms, p99 and max 600 ms, 200 calls. Hedge at 80 ms: p50 still 40, p99 and max 120 ms (80 ms of waiting plus a 40 ms hedge), 210 calls. With the hedge at 30 ms, every request is hedged: 400 calls, twice the load, for a p99 that the 80 ms hedge already got down to 120. A hedge time below the normal time duplicates every request. The Java twin uses Reactor's Mono.firstWithValue and prints about the same numbers in real time, give or take the scheduling delays of a busy machine.

sections.h: Turn work away at the door, then close in order
sections.html:
Northline takes 10 calls at a time, at 50 ms each, so within a 300 ms deadline it can answer about 60 requests. A burst of 500 then leaves hundreds waiting for a permit, until they fail at the deadline anyway. This section's demo measured it: 50 live answers, 450 misses, and 135,000 ms of waiting, summed over the requests that missed, that produced nothing.

Customers don't read slips. Like the oven thermometer in Backpressure in practice, they arrive whenever they like, so someone has to choose what to lose. Buffering: buffer, conflate, collectLatest and fusion asked the same question at the shelf in the hatch: when the shelf is full, either the cook waits or a dumpling goes in the bin. Waiting is the queue we just measured. The bin is closer to the answer, with one change: the customer hears about it. Load shedding turns away work the service can't finish in time, at once and with a clear word. QuoteService admits at most maxInFlight requests, and the next one gets a failed future straight away, which lesson 1's handler writes as 7 ERR busy:

Java
// Java equivalent: the same door with a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore
public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String destination) {
    if (!accepting) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new ShuttingDownException());
    if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new BusyException());
    CompletableFuture<Quote> reply = best(destination).toFuture();
    reply.whenComplete((q, e) -> admission.release());
    return reply;
}
Kotlin
override fun quote(destination: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> {
    if (!accepting) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(ShuttingDownException())
    if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(BusyException())   // never waits
    val reply = scope.future { best.quote(destination) }
    reply.whenComplete { _, _ -> admission.release() }         // however the request ends
    return reply
}

With 50 admitted, the same burst got the same 50 live answers, and the other 450 customers heard busy within a millisecond, early enough to try another post office. tryAcquire takes a permit if one is free and never waits, so the event loop that calls quote never waits either. The permit comes back in whenComplete, however the request ends, including a cancel after a hang-up. Here the picture breaks in our favour: a dumpling in the bin is gone for good, while a customer who hears "busy" can ask again elsewhere.

A request that can't make its deadline fails either way. Fail it at the door, in a millisecond.

Shutdown uses the same pieces. Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown closed the kitchen at night in a fixed order, and the post office closes the same way. Lock the front door, stop taking new questions, let the customers at the counter finish, send the rest away, then turn off the lights:

Java
// Java equivalent for an executor-based service: the same order, from "Pools in production"
void shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException {
    server.stopAccepting();                                      // 1. no new connections
    accepting = false;                                           // 2. stop admitting
    pool.shutdown();
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), MILLISECONDS)) {   // 3. drain, up to grace
        pool.shutdownNow();                                      // 4. interrupt the rest
        pool.awaitTermination(5, SECONDS);
    }
    server.close();                                              // 5. close connections, stop the loops
}
Kotlin
suspend fun shutdown(grace: Duration): Int {
    accepting = false                                            // 2. stop admitting
    val job = scope.coroutineContext.job
    withTimeoutOrNull(grace) { job.children.toList().joinAll() }   // 3. drain, up to grace
    val left = job.children.count()
    job.cancelAndJoin()                                          // 4. cancel the rest, wait for them
    return left
}

// QuoteApp: 1. server.stopAccepting(), then the above, then 5. server.close()

That order has a name, a graceful shutdown: no new work, a grace period for the work in flight to finish, then cancel the rest and release everything. First, the server stops accepting connections (1). Then the service stops admitting requests, which now get ERR shutting down (2). The requests in flight get the grace period (3). What is left is cancelled, and cancelAndJoin() waits until those coroutines have finished their cleanup, so that no coroutine outlives the service (4). Finally, the server closes the connections and stops its loops (5). Lesson 1's ChannelGroup pays off here: each connection is closed on its own loop, behind the reply that the drain just let through.

That's the whole service. Before we call it done, a reviewer has a fair question.

try.title: Queue the burst, or turn it away
steps: Open ShedDemo.kt. A burst of 500 requests meets a courier that takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, under a 300 ms deadline.
Predict the live answers, the misses, the requests turned away as busy, and the time spent waiting for nothing, for both runs.
Run it. Then admit 100 instead of 50 and predict the misses again.

code.title: ShedDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** * A burst of 500 requests. The provider takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, and every request * has a 300 ms deadline. Queue them all, or shed what can't make the deadline? */ fun main() = runTest { for (maxInFlight in listOf(null, 50)) { val provider = Semaphore(10) val admission = maxInFlight?.let { Semaphore(it) } var live = 0 var late = 0 var busy = 0 var waitedForNothing = 0L coroutineScope { repeat(500) { launch { if (admission != null && !admission.tryAcquire()) { busy++ // answered "ERR busy" at once return@launch } try { val start = currentTime val answer = withTimeoutOrNull(300) { provider.withPermit { delay(50) } } if (answer != null) live++ else { late++; waitedForNothing += currentTime - start } } finally { admission?.release() } } } } println("%-14s live answers: %3d missed the deadline: %3d shed as busy: %3d ms spent waiting for nothing: %,d".format( if (maxInFlight == null) "queue them all" else "admit $maxInFlight", live, late, busy, waitedForNothing)) } }

alt.title: ShedDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent with virtual threads: Semaphore.tryAcquire() sheds, a timed tryAcquire is the deadline package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * A burst of 500 requests. The provider takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, and every request * has a 300 ms deadline. Queue them all, or shed what can't make the deadline? Real time. */ public class ShedDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer maxInFlight : new Integer[] {null, 50}) { Semaphore provider = new Semaphore(10); Semaphore admission = maxInFlight == null ? null : new Semaphore(maxInFlight); AtomicInteger live = new AtomicInteger(), late = new AtomicInteger(), busy = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicLong waitedForNothing = new AtomicLong(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (admission != null && !admission.tryAcquire()) { busy.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // ERR busy long start = System.nanoTime(); try { long deadline = start + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(300); if (provider.tryAcquire(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } finally { provider.release(); } if (System.nanoTime() <= deadline) { live.incrementAndGet(); return null; } } late.incrementAndGet(); waitedForNothing.addAndGet((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); } finally { if (admission != null) admission.release(); } return null; }); } } System.out.printf("%-14s live answers: %3d missed the deadline: %3d shed as busy: %3d ms spent waiting for nothing: %,d%n", maxInFlight == null ? "queue them all" : "admit " + maxInFlight, live.get(), late.get(), busy.get(), waitedForNothing.get()); } } }

try.expect: Queue them all: 50 live answers, 450 misses, and 135,000 ms spent waiting by requests that got nothing. Admit 50: the same 50 live answers, 0 misses, 450 turned away at once, and no wasted waiting. Admitting 100 gives the same 50 live answers, 50 misses and 15,000 ms of wasted waiting: past what the courier can serve in 300 ms, a bigger door only buys slow failures. The Java twin does the same with virtual threads in real time, so its waiting total drifts a little (139,688 ms in one run here).

sections.h: Design review: would one virtual thread per connection be simpler?
sections.html:
Here is the finished design next to the question every reviewer asks about it: wouldn't one virtual thread per connection, with plain blocking calls to the couriers, be simpler? A virtual thread is a thread the JDK makes so cheap that a program can run thousands of them, and blocking means a call that holds its thread until the answer comes.

Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem offered the post office two ways out of the crowd: fewer clerks, or cheaper clerks. This service took the first way: a few clerks, each watching a row of boxes, who never wait. Virtual threads take the second: a clerk for every customer, so cheap that most of them can stand and wait. Here are the two side by side:

Concern This service One virtual thread per connection
idle connections a few loop threads hold thousands one parked virtual thread each, a few KB
waiting for couriers suspended coroutines blocked virtual threads
deadline and cancel structured: the cancel reaches every courier call interrupts, which some blocking clients ignore
limits per courier a Semaphore per courier a Semaphore per courier
framing and backpressure Netty's decoders and auto-read your own read loop; TCP does the pacing
code shape futures at the Java edge, coroutines inside plain blocking Java

Virtual threads make the right-hand column cheap (The thread-per-request wall), and for many services they are the better choice. Switch when the couriers only ship blocking clients, such as JDBC, Java's standard way to talk to a database. This design would then need a pool of blocking threads behind the coroutines, and you'd pay for two models. Switch, too, when the team writes Java and connections number in the thousands. Stay on the event loop when the service already lives on Netty or a framework built on it, such as Vert.x or Quarkus; when connections number in the hundreds of thousands; when you need the control over the protocol that auto-read and decoders give you; or when the courier clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them.

Either way, the limits stay. Bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown appear in both columns. Moving to virtual threads removes the pool, and with it the one limit nobody wrote down, as Moving a blocking service to virtual threads found. The question that picks the model is where the waiting happens, as Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model put it. Here it happens in three courier calls per request, under a deadline, and both models can wait well.

Pick the model by where the waiting happens. Keep the limits whichever you pick.

aside.title: Where do these guards live in a real service?
aside.html: Often in a library rather than in hand-written code. Resilience4j, for example, is a Java library with a bulkhead, a retry with backoff, a time limit and a circuit breaker, a switch that stops calling a courier that keeps failing. Whichever you use, let one layer own the retries. Two retries in the courier's own client, two in a library and two in your code turn one call into 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls during an outage. And when a platform stops your program, tell it to send no more customers before the drain starts, so the shutdown order holds.

compare.title: The guards around a courier with coroutines and on virtual threads

java.title: GuardedProvider.java (virtual threads)
java.html: // Java on virtual threads: the same guards around a blocking courier client final class GuardedProvider { private final BlockingProvider delegate; private final Semaphore permits; private final Backoff backoff; GuardedProvider(BlockingProvider delegate, int maxConcurrent, Backoff backoff) { this.delegate = delegate; this.permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); this.backoff = backoff; } Quote quote(String destination) throws IOException, InterruptedException { if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once(destination); // 2. never repeat a booking for (int n = 1; ; n++) { try { return once(destination); } catch (IOException e) { if (n > backoff.retries()) throw e; // out of retries double factor = 1 + backoff.jitter() * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1); Thread.sleep((long) (backoff.nominal(n).toMillis() * factor)); // an interrupt ends it } } } private Quote once(String destination) throws IOException, InterruptedException { permits.acquire(); // 1. every call holds a permit try { return delegate.quote(destination); } finally { permits.release(); } } }

kotlin.title: Resilience.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun <T> retrying(backoff: Backoff, random: Random, call: suspend () -> T): T { var n = 0 while (true) { try { return call() } catch (e: IOException) { if (++n > backoff.retries) throw e // out of retries val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor) // so callers that failed together spread out } } } class GuardedProvider( private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int, private val backoff: Backoff = Backoff(), private val hedgeAfter: Duration? = null, private val random: Random = Random.Default, ) : Provider { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) override val name: String get() = delegate.name override val idempotent: Boolean get() = delegate.idempotent override suspend fun quote(destination: String): Quote { val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(destination) } } // 1. every call holds a permit if (!delegate.idempotent) return once() // 2. never repeat a booking val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) }) return retrying(backoff, random, attempt) // 3. a hedge per attempt } }

compare.note: The rules are the same in both: a permit around every single call, one call for a courier that isn't idempotent, and retries with jitter for IOException only. What differs is what waiting and stopping cost. In Kotlin, withPermit and delay suspend, so a thousand requests waiting for a permit or a backoff hold no threads, and a cancel (the deadline or a hang-up) reaches them at once through the job tree. On virtual threads, acquire and Thread.sleep block, which is cheap too, and a cancel is an interrupt: it reaches the sleep and the semaphore, but it reaches the courier call only if its client responds to interrupts. The Java version leaves the hedge out. On threads, a hedge takes an ExecutorCompletionService, or JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope, still a preview API there (Structured concurrency and scoped values), and the loser is stopped by an interrupt, which again works only if its client listens. Java code that can block on a virtual thread is shorter to read. Kotlin code gets the hedge and the deadline from the library.

lab.title: Bulkheads, retries, a hedge, shedding and shutdown
steps: Run the tests. All 13 fail. The l03 package already holds lessons 1 and 2's solutions; Provider now has idempotent, and QuoteApp.kt wires the server, the service and the shutdown order.

Write GuardedProvider.quote (points 1 to 3 of its KDoc): a Semaphore field, a permit around every single call, one call for a courier that isn't idempotent, retrying for the rest, and hedged around each attempt when hedgeAfter is set.
Add the jitter to retrying: one line that computes the factor, and the delay that uses it.
Write hedged as its KDoc describes. The bulkhead, retry and hedge tests should pass now.
In QuoteService, add the admission Semaphore and the accepting flag to quote, then write shutdown. Run the tests until all 13 pass, including the two over TCP, then run them twice more.
hints: If the bulkhead test sees more than 4 calls at once, the permit isn't around every call. If the limit counts hedges too sees 2, the hedge runs outside the permit: wrap the permit inside the function you pass to hedged.

select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } } is in kotlinx.coroutines.selects. Without coroutineContext.cancelChildren() after it, coroutineScope waits for the slow call, and the hedge test reads 1,000 ms instead of 130.
Semaphore.tryAcquire() never suspends, so quote can call it on the event loop. Release in whenComplete on the returned future, so a request that is cancelled gives its permit back too.
In shutdown, join a snapshot of the children inside withTimeoutOrNull(grace), count what is still running, then cancelAndJoin() the scope's job.
lab.done: All 13 tests in UnderLoadTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the hedge from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T: start the call, and if it hasn't answered after after, start one more, return the first answer and stop the other. Which line, if you leave it out, makes the hedge useless, and why?

answer.html: suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope { val first = async { call() } val early = withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } // stop waiting, not the call if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early val second = async { call() } val winner = select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } } coroutineContext.cancelChildren() // or coroutineScope waits for the loser winner }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor <T> Mono<T> hedged(Duration after, Mono<T> call) { return Mono.firstWithValue(call, Mono.delay(after).then(call)); // the loser is cancelled }

recap: Give each courier its own bulkhead, a Semaphore sized from its contract by Little's law, with a permit around every single call, hedges included.
Retry only idempotent calls, only errors a later attempt can fix, with jitter and inside the deadline. A price that is really a booking, like Fjord's, is asked for once.
Hedge the courier whose tail hurts, after about its p95, and cancel the loser. In the demo, p99 fell from 600 to 120 ms for 5% more calls.

Turn work away at the door with tryAcquire: a request that can't make the deadline gets ERR busy in a millisecond instead of failing after 300 ms in a queue. Then shut down in order: stop accepting, stop admitting, drain, cancelAndJoin the rest, close.

Event loop or virtual threads, the limits stay. Switch to virtual threads when the courier clients only block or the team writes plain Java; keep the event loop for huge numbers of connections, control over the protocol and non-blocking clients.

Where this design stops: fixed limits are right only for the load they were measured under, and retries make a courier that is down worse. Circuit breakers, retry budgets and adaptive limits come next (Go deeper).

explain.prompt: Design review. A doubtful reviewer says: "This is too much machinery: Netty, coroutines, futures, semaphores, hedges. One virtual thread per connection with blocking courier clients would be simpler, and Netty buffers everything anyway." Defend your design: say what each guard protects against, what you would keep if you did switch to virtual threads, and when you would switch.
explain.answer: Each piece answers a failure we can name. The event loop never waits, and auto-read with a cap of 16 per connection keeps one greedy client from filling our memory, because Netty's buffers have no limit of their own. The fan-out asks three couriers under one deadline in a supervisor scope, so a failed or slow courier just drops out, and a stale price, clearly labelled, beats no answer. Cancelling the future on hang-up cancels every courier call through the job tree. Under load, each courier gets a bulkhead sized from its contract, so we never send Northline more than its 10 calls; only idempotent couriers are retried, with jitter so a recovering courier isn't hit by waves of retries, and Fjord, whose prices are bookings, is asked once. Northline's slow tail gets a hedge after its p95, which cut p99 from 600 to 120 ms for 5% more calls. Admission turns away what we can't answer in 300 ms with an immediate ERR busy instead of a slow failure, and shutdown stops intake, drains, cancels and joins the rest, and then closes, so nothing leaks. If we switched to virtual threads, I'd keep every limit: the bulkheads, the deadline, admission and the shutdown order, because virtual threads remove the pool and with it the only limit we never wrote down. I'd switch if the couriers only had blocking clients, because then this design needs a blocking pool anyway, or if the team prefers plain Java and connections stay in the thousands. I'd stay on Netty for huge numbers of connections, for the control over the protocol, or when the courier clients are non-blocking and cancellation has to reach them.

deeper.html:
What a production version of this service would add, roughly in the order it would hurt to miss them.

Measurements. For each courier: how long calls take (the hedge time comes from the p95), permits in use, calls retried, hedges sent and won, errors by type. For the service: requests admitted, turned away and served stale, and the age of the stale prices. Without them, every number in this track (the 10 permits, the 80 ms hedge, the 50 in flight) is a guess.

A circuit breaker. Retries help with short blips; they make a courier that is down worse. A circuit breaker counts recent failures and, past a threshold, stops calling the courier for a while, then lets a few trial calls through. It sits outside the retry loop, so an open breaker fails fast instead of retrying.

A retry budget. Cap retries as a share of all calls, for example 10%. During a long outage the budget runs out, and the service stops multiplying its own load.

Adaptive limits. Fixed permits are right only for the load they were measured under. Adaptive limits change the number of permits from the response times they observe, the way TCP finds out how much the network can carry: when calls slow down, the limit shrinks before the courier falls over.

Deadlines and context passed along. Send the time left with each courier call, so that the courier can give up too, and carry each request's id across the edge between Netty and coroutines (asContextElement or MDCContext, as Dispatchers and the coroutine context showed), so that a slow price can be found in the logs.

Fair admission. One heavy client can still take most of the 50 places. A quota per client at the door, on top of the limit for the whole service, keeps a single caller from crowding out the rest.

A plan for shutdown on a shared platform. Programs that run as many copies behind a load balancer, a router that spreads customers over the copies, should first tell it to send no more customers, then drain, and keep the grace period shorter than the time the platform waits before it stops the program by force.
